notes: Help page example fits rma(yi, vi, test='knha') separately on the Males and Females rows (Lehmann, Elliot and Calin-Jageman 2018, Evol Psychol; OSF xy47p), each with only the effect-level random effect of rma. The first rows show one experiment (Short_Title, e.g. Roberts et al., 2010 - Exp 2) with a Females and a Males row, although the page calls the column unique, so Short_Title is the unit the rows repeat within, rendered as a random intercept, and Gender carries the page's split. yi is the standardized mean difference, vi its sampling variance; the source weights each effect by vi, which the formula leaves out. The group Ns, means and SDs, SD_diff, RM_r and pooled compute yi; Control_Attractiveness is computed from Control_M. RULE GAP: the page's rma fits name no grouping; the repeated experiment is counted as a cluster the source treats as independent, so published_model no.

formula: cbind(resp, n - resp) ~ 0 + factor(id) + int + (1 | id) + (1 | id:int)
notes: Help page example: pairwise(treat = int, event = resp, n = n, studlab = paste(author, year), reference = 'plac', sm = 'OR') turns the arms into log odds ratios per comparison; netmeta(pw, reference.group = 'placebo', common = FALSE) fits a random-effects network meta-analysis, and netcomb an additive component NMA. netmeta's random-effects model is rma.mv's random = ~ comp | study with rho = 1/2 (the dat.senn2013 page fits both and attributes the difference to the tau estimator); on the arms it is the arm-based model with fixed study effects and compound-symmetric arm effects, written as (1 | id) + (1 | id:int) with equal variances, id:int one arm per row. 93 trials of 2 to 4 arms (Linde et al. 2016, J Clin Epidemiol; Ruecker et al. 2020). int.long spells out int; author and year label the trial. RULE GAP: netmeta is not on the brief's list of mixed-model calls; filed yes as the random-effects NMA it fits, rendered on the arm table.

Help page example: to.wide(dat, study='study', grp='treatment', ref='TAU', grpvars=c('diff','se','n')) turns these arms into contrasts yi = diff1 - diff2 against each study's TAU (or first) arm, vi = se1^2 + se2^2, V with the shared arm's covariance; rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + No.treatment + Wait.list + Placebo + F2F.CBT + Hybrid.CBT + Multimedia.CBT, random = ~ comp | study, rho=1/2). On this arm table the contrast model is the arm-based model with fixed study effects (differencing removes them) and compound-symmetric arm effects, written as (1 | study) + (1 | study:treatment) with equal variances, as the dat.senn2013 page fits it on arms; study:treatment is one arm per row. Further fits: random inconsistency effects (list(~ comp | study, ~ comp | design)), the CBT forms collapsed, and a component NMA CBT:(multi + cog + ba + psed + home + prob + soc + relax + goal + final). diff is the arm's standardized mean change, se its standard error, which the source weights by; intensity = sessions x length. Lopez-Lopez et al. 2019, Psychol Med. RULE GAP: the documented model is fitted on contrasts built from this table and rendered on its arms.

Help page example: rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ condition, random = list(~ 1 | article/experiment/sample/id, ~ 1 | pairing), data=dat, sparse=TRUE), then robust(res, cluster=article, clubSandwich=TRUE) (McCurdy et al. 2020, Psychon Bull Rev). yi is a condition's mean recall rate, vi its sampling variance; the source weights each mean by vi, which the formula leaves out. The nesting expands to article, article:experiment, article:experiment:sample and the row id; experiment and sample are numbered within their parents, hence the composite terms; id is one level per row (observation level), its column ignored and its term kept. pairing links a read condition to its generate conditions within an experiment. ni (participants per condition) enters vi. The coded moderators (gen_difficulty to retention_delay) are not in this model.

Help page example: escalc(measure='ZCOR', ri=Correlation, ni=SampleSize), so yi = atanh(Correlation) with vi = 1/(SampleSize - 3), which the source weights by; rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | StudyID). StudyID has one level per row (Sparrow01, Sparrow02, ...), so the page's term is observation level. Place (the study population) repeats (Hungary1 and Norway1 twice in the first rows); Nakagawa et al. (2007, Behav Ecol) propose a meta-analysis method that accounts for non-independence of the data (abstract; paper not read), so Place is rendered as a random intercept. RULE GAP: the page's random term is observation level; the repeated population is counted as a cluster, published_model no.

formula: I(cases / total * 100) ~ I(bmi - ave(bmi, study)) + (1 | study/grp)
notes: Help page example: escalc(measure='PR', xi=cases, ni=total) converted to percent (yi*100, vi*100^2), bmicent <- bmi - ave(bmi, study), rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ bmicent, random = ~ 1 | study/grp) (O'Brien, Ray and Chan 2003, Epidemiology). grp numbers the BMI groups within a study, one row per study:grp (observation level), so grp is ignored and its term kept. The source fits the percentage as a normal outcome weighted by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Further fits on the page: random = ~ bmicent | study with struct='GEN' (a random slope on the same grouping, not a row) and a restricted cubic spline rcs(bmicent, 4). bmi is the interval midpoint, bmi.lb and bmi.ub its bounds; ch, dm and mg are study-level exclusion criteria. RULE GAP: a Gaussian model of a binomial share on the identity scale has no Family entry for a binomial response; family left blank.

formula: log(xi / (ni - xi)) ~ 0 + factor(study) + trt + (1 | study) + (1 | study:trt)
notes: Help page example: escalc(measure='PLO', xi=xi, ni=ni) gives each arm's log odds and its sampling variance; trt releveled to control; rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + factor(study) + trt, random = ~ trt | study, rho=1/2), an arm-based random-effects network meta-analysis with fixed study effects (Pagliaro et al. 1992, Ann Intern Med). random = ~ trt | study with rho fixed at 1/2 is a compound-symmetric arm effect, written as (1 | study) + (1 | study:trt) with equal variances; study:trt is one arm per row. study is both the fixed study effect and the grouping factor; the grouping stands. The arm's log odds is fitted as normal with its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out; the binomial logit is its exact-likelihood form, so family is blank. 26 trials with 2 or 3 arms; the page also runs rma.mh per comparison on the to.wide contrasts.

Help page fits two univariate rma(yi, sei=sei, method='DL') on the DFS and the OS rows. The cited source Riley et al. (2007, Stat Med 26:78-97; erratum Riley 2011) fits a bivariate random-effects meta-analysis of the two log hazard ratios with correlated study effects per outcome (abstract read: BRMA compared with univariate fits on two examples), in metafor terms rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, random = ~ outcome | study, struct='UN'), written as (outcome | study). 81 studies, 17 with both outcomes. vi is the sampling variance (sei its root), which the source weights by; the within-study correlation the bivariate model needs is not in the table. Model recalled from the cited paper, not fitted on the page.

Help page only plots the dose-toxicity curves per study (12 phase I studies of irinotecan and S-1, several doses each). Roever et al. (2022, Stat Med 41:3915-3940; abstract read) propose a two-stage approach: penalized logistic regression of dose-limiting toxicity on dose within each study, then a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of the per-study estimates. Its one-stage counterpart is the logistic GLMM written here with study random intercepts and log-dose slopes (the log-dose scale recalled, not read); the two-stage fit is not a mixed model on this table, so published_model no. Ursino et al. (2021) fit a one-stage hierarchical model to the sorafenib twin dat.ursino2021.

Help page example: escalc(measure='MN', mi=mi, sdi=sdi, ni=ni) gives each arm's mean with vi = sdi^2/ni; treatment releveled to placebo; res.re <- rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + study + treatment, random = ~ treatment | study, rho=1/2), an arm-based random-effects network meta-analysis with fixed study effects (res.fe drops the random term). random = ~ treatment | study with rho fixed at 1/2 is a compound-symmetric arm effect, written as (1 | study) + (1 | study:treatment) with equal variances; study:treatment is one arm per row; study is both the fixed effect and the grouping factor, the grouping stands. The source weights each arm by vi, which the formula leaves out. The page also fits the contrast-based model on to.wide contrasts (random = ~ comp | study, rho=1/2) and random inconsistency effects (~ comp | design), and computes P-scores (Senn et al. 2013; Law et al. 2016; Ruecker and Schwarzer 2015). 26 trials, one with three arms. comment says whether mi is the follow-up HbA1c mean or its change from baseline.

formula: yi ~ ave(aget1, studyid) * ave(aget2, studyid) + sexmix + (1 | studyid/esid)
notes: Help page examples: aget1 and aget2 replaced by their study means (ave(..., studyid)); esid <- 1:nrow(dat), the row number (no column); V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=studyid, obs=esid, rho=0.8); rma.mv(yi, V, random = ~ esid | studyid), then rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ aget1 + aget2, then aget1 * aget2, then aget1 * aget2 + sexmix, random = ~ 1 | studyid/esid), each with robust(res, cluster=studyid, clubSandwich=TRUE) (Tanner-Smith, Tipton and Polanin 2016). The last model's terms are filed; the grouping is the same throughout. esid is one level per row (observation level). yi is the r-to-z correlation and vi its sampling variance (sei its root), which the source weights by with an assumed within-study correlation of 0.8; the formula leaves both out. propmale is not modelled.

formula: cbind(deaths, n - deaths) ~ factor(study) + group + (0 + group | study)
notes: Help page example: pairwise(treat = group, event = deaths, n = n, studlab = study, sm = 'OR'), then metabin with method = 'glmm', model = 'CM.AL', random = TRUE, a random-effects conditional logistic GLMM (metafor's rma.glmm with the approximate hypergeometric likelihood), beside IV, Mantel-Haenszel, Peto and penalized logistic fits (Tian et al. 2009, Biostatistics). Conditioning on each trial's total events stands for fixed study effects, with a random treatment effect per study: written as factor(study) + group + (0 + group | study), filed as an uncorrelated slope. 48 two-arm trials of rosiglitazone vs control; the six double-zero trials it adds are what separates it from dat.nissen2007. infarcts is the other outcome (Nissen and Wolski's primary), not modelled on the page; n.all counts all patients, n those with outcome data. intervention and detailed.intervention name the arm's drugs.

Help page only plots the dose-toxicity curves per study (13 phase I trials of sorafenib, several doses each). The cited source Ursino, Roever, Zohar and Friede (2021, Ann Appl Stat 15:174-193; abstract read) fits a Bayesian curve-free hierarchical model on the logistic scale to these trials: a toxicity probability per dose with study random effects that follow an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Gaussian process over doses, priors from a latent Gamma process. Rendered as a dose factor with a study random intercept; the process over doses is not representable. Roever et al. (2022) fit a two-stage penalized logistic regression and random-effects meta-analysis to both datasets (see dat.roever2022). Model recalled from the cited paper, not fitted on the page; its priors are given in words only.

Help page example: escalc(measure='ZCOR', ri=r, ni=n), so yi = atanh(r) with vi = 1/(n - 3); rma.mv(yi, vi, random = list(~ 1 | study_id, ~ 1 | obs)) (White 2020, Biol Lett). obs is one level per row (observation level), its column ignored and its term kept. The source weights each effect by vi, which the formula leaves out. The moderators (exp_obs, control, class, genus, species, sex, iridescent, col_var, col_component, quality_measure, region) are not in this model.

formula: cbind(r, N - r) ~ 0 + factor(author) + treatment + (1 | author) + (1 | author:treatment)
notes: Help page example: pairwise(treatment, event = r, n = N, studlab = author, sm = 'OR'); netmeta(pw) fits the common- and random-effects network meta-analysis, rendered on the arms as for dat.linde2016 (fixed study effects, compound-symmetric arm effects, author:treatment one arm per row). Three trials (Boyd 1997, Calverly 2003 with four arms, Celli 2003), so author has three levels. Woods, Hawkins and Scott (2010, BMC Med Res Methodol) fit a Bayesian NMA of these counts on the log-hazard scale. RULE GAP: netmeta is not on the brief's list of mixed-model calls, and the grouping has only three levels.

psymetadata documents the data only (no example, no vignette): 85 Fisher-z effect sizes of the out-group entitativity and prejudice relation from 21 studies (study_id), es_id one per row. Agadullina and Lovakov (2018, Br J Soc Psychol 57:703-731) pool 85 effects from 33 independent samples (abstract via search); their model was not read (paywalled). Effects nested in studies rendered as a three-level model, es_id the observation-level term. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by; n enters it. RULE GAP: the paper's model is unread, so published_model no.

psymetadata documents the data only (no example, no vignette; source OSF jhavp): 637 Hedges' g effect sizes of Cogmed working-memory training from 48 studies (study_id), es_id one per row, moderators transfer, test, allocation, comparison, baseline, age group and population. Aksayli, Sala and Gobet (2019, Educ Res Rev 27:229-243) not read (full text unavailable); the group's other meta-analyses use robust variance estimation. Effects nested in studies rendered as a three-level model. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by; ni enters it. RULE GAP: the paper's model is unread, so published_model no.

psymetadata documents the data only (no example, no vignette; OSF 5admx): 747 Fisher-z effect sizes of the math anxiety and math achievement relation, study_id corresponding to author, es_id one per row, moderators continent, grade, low_ability and teachers. Barroso et al. (2021, Psychol Bull 147:134-168; PubMed abstract) report r = -.28 over 747 effects with grade and math ability as moderators; the model section was not read (PMC page blocked). Effects nested in studies rendered as a three-level model. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by; ni enters it. RULE GAP: the paper's model is unread, so published_model no.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF v8kxb): 286 Cohen's d effect sizes of facial feedback on emotional experience from 138 studies (study_id), es_id one per row. Coles, Larsen and Lench (2019, Psychol Bull 145:610-651; PubMed abstract): random effects meta-regression with robust variance estimates, effects clustered by study; rendered as a study random intercept, as the registry renders a GEE cluster. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by. title names the publication. RULE GAP: robust variance estimation is not on the brief's list of mixed-model calls; filed yes by the GEE precedent.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF 5wjb2): 89 correlations of future-thinking specificity with depression from 46 studies (study_id), samples within studies (samp_id), es_id one per row, moderators sex, age, depression status, valence and design. Gamble et al. (2019, Perspect Psychol Sci 14:816-834; PubMed abstract): random-effects meta-analytic modelling, valence and sex as moderators; how dependent effects were modelled was not read. Rendered with the page's study and sample levels. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by. RULE GAP: the paper's model is unread, so published_model no.

psymetadata documents the data only: 67 standardized mean differences of red vs a control color on test performance, study_id (22 per the page) and es_id one per row. Gnambs (2020, Psychon Bull Rev 27:1374-1382; PMC7704521, method read): the effect sizes were pooled using a random-effects model with REML in metafor, and because some studies provided more than one effect size, a multivariate meta-analysis was specified that acknowledged the sampling covariances (Gleser and Olkin); tau^2 is reported between the 38 independent samples, which have no column, so study_id (the publication holding them) stands in. Moderators were the control color, color matching, presentation and the cognitive measure. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF jv7wt); its title and description are copied from noble2019, but the data are 1,194 Hedges' g effects of bilingual vs monolingual children's executive functioning. Lowe et al. (2021, Psychol Sci 32:1115-1146; PMC8641133, Multilevel model section and Table 2 read): effect sizes are not independent, so a multilevel model was built with levels for comparisons within experiments, experiments within studies and studies within research groups; Table 2 adds Participants, Study and Research group in turn, each improving AIC and the likelihood-ratio test, and the four-level model is final. The columns participants (participant pairs), study_id and lab_group are those levels, es_id the effect. subsample and clusters code other dependencies the final model leaves out. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF hnmy4): 1,246 correlations of emotional intelligence with academic performance from 158 studies (study_id) and their samples (sample_id); the es_id the page lists is not in the table. MacCann et al. (2020, Psychol Bull 146:150-186; PubMed abstract): an overall rho = .20 using robust variance estimation, moderators EI stream, subject and achievement type; the cluster level was not read, so study and sample are rendered as random intercepts, as the registry renders a GEE cluster. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by. RULE GAP: robust variance estimation is not on the brief's list of mixed-model calls; filed yes by the GEE precedent.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF bcywg): 1,268 Hedges' g age differences in executive functioning (younger vs older groups) from 431 studies (study_id), es_id one per row, by EF domain, Miyake framework and task. Maldonado et al. (2020, J Gerontol B 75:e31-e55; PubMed abstract) meta-analyse at the task, subdomain and global EF level; the model was not read. Proposed: effects nested in studies with the EF domain as covariate. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by; n1, n2 and n_total enter it. RULE GAP: the paper's model is unread, so published_model no.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF ux3eh): a subset of Many Labs 2 (Klein et al. 2018, Adv Methods Pract Psychol Sci), one effect per replicating lab (lab) and replicated finding (analysis), in r (yi_r, vi_r) and in d (yi_d, vi_d, the same effect on another scale). The paper meta-analyses each finding across samples (not read here), so rows repeat within lab across findings, crossed; lab is rendered as a random intercept and the finding as a covariate. Lab-level moderators: country, weird, western, educated, industrialized, rich, democratic, mean_weird_score, online. vi_r is the sampling variance, which the source weights by. RULE GAP: per-finding fits treat the labs as independent; the lab counted as a cluster, published_model no.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF 34xyw): 316 Hedges' g effects of shared reading on children's language from 54 studies (study_id), es_id one per row, moderators measure, age, ses, experimenter, duration, dialogic_reading and follow_up. Noble et al. (2019, Educ Res Rev 28:100290; full text read): we used robust variance estimation (RVE) with hierarchical weights and small-sample corrections to calculate the overall effect size and run meta-regression (Hedges, Tipton and Johnson 2010), the effect sizes of one study forming one cluster, in the robumeta R package. The hierarchical working model has a between-study and a within-study variance, rendered as study and effect random intercepts, as the registry renders a GEE cluster. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by. RULE GAP: robust variance estimation is not on the brief's list of mixed-model calls; filed yes by the GEE precedent.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF fq5wp): 2,443 Fisher-z effects from 131 meta-analyses of intelligence research, study_id indexing the meta-analysis, es_id the effect, es and se the effect on its original scale (type_es). Nuijten et al. (2020, J Intell 8:36; PMC7720125, method read): a two-step strategy, a random-effects meta-regression on the standard error within each meta-analysis with rma() in metafor (Paule-Mandel), then a random-effects meta-analysis of the per-meta-analysis coefficients; a multilevel model of primary studies nested in meta-analyses was tried but failed to converge (footnote 2). Proposed: the effects nested in meta-analyses. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF qk2vu): 1,555 Hedges' g effects of cognitive training on near and far transfer, study_id indexing the first-order meta-analysis, es_id the effect, author the primary study, comparison the control type, model which of the paper's three models uses the row. Sala et al. (2019, Collabra Psychol 5:18) is a second-order meta-analysis (Models 1 to 3: working-memory training near and far transfer, other trainings); its model was not read (full text unavailable). Proposed: effects nested in meta-analyses; primary studies may recur across meta-analyses through author, not filed. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by. RULE GAP: the paper's model is unread, so published_model no.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF mrxhe): 75 Hedges' g effects of tDCS on inhibitory control (go/no-go and stop-signal tasks), study_id (62 per the page, 45 studies per the abstract) and es_id one per row, moderators design, control, blinding, task, population, polarity, intensity, electrode placements and timing. Schroeder et al. (2020, Brain Stimul 13:1159-1167; PubMed abstract): g = 0.21 moderated by electrode placement and task; the model was not read. Effects nested in studies rendered as a three-level model. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by. RULE GAP: the paper's model is unread, so published_model no.

psymetadata documents the data only (PsyArXiv gjqcs): 99 Hedges' g effects of executive function in intellectual disability vs mental-age-matched controls from 26 studies (study_id), es_id one per row, group_id the aetiology (NSID, FXS, DS, WS), ef_type, ef_component, domain and test. Spaniol and Danielsson (2022, J Intellect Disabil Res 66:9-31; PubMed abstract): a multilevel random-effects meta-analysis, g = -0.34, aetiology a significant moderator; the levels were not read, rendered as effects nested in studies. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF szfwx): 76 correlations of learning goal orientation with performance adaptation from 35 studies (study_id), es_id one per row; stasielowicz2019b holds the performance goal orientation effects. Stasielowicz (2019, J Res Pers 82:103847; abstract via search): three-level meta-analyses were conducted for learning goal orientation and performance goal orientation, rendered as effects nested in studies. age_imputed fills age. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by; n enters it.

Stasielowicz (2019, J Res Pers 82:103847; abstract via search): three-level meta-analyses for learning and performance goal orientation, rendered as effects nested in studies; whether pgo_type splits the fits was not read. age_imputed fills age. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by; n enters it.

Stramaccia et al. (2021, J Exp Psychol Gen 150:828-850; PubMed abstract) estimate the effect per cluster (healthy 0.28, anxious -0.21, depressed 0.05, repressive 0.42) and by instruction type; the model was not read. psymetadata documents the data only and cites Assink and Wibbelink (2016, Quant Methods Psychol 12(3):154; PDF read), a tutorial on this 17-study, 100-effect subset of Wibbelink et al.'s juvenile recidivism meta-analysis: overall <- rma.mv(y, v, random = list(~ 1 | effectsizeID, ~ 1 | studyID), tdist=TRUE, ...), a three-level model, then the moderators fitted one at a time (publication status, recidivism type dummies, publication year). study_id and es_id are the tutorial's studyID and effectsizeID, yi its Cohen's d (y), vi its sampling variance (v), which the source weights by. pstatnotpub is 1 - pstatpub.
